utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not present. Mr. Mladic, the Defence has waived the right of Mr. Mladic to be present yesterday and today. Therefore, we'll proceed. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I raise the following issue. The Chamber notes that yesterday in the 1st of November, the Prosecution has filed an urgent motion to add 13 exhibits to its 65 ter exhibit list which are to be used during the testimony of Richard Philips. Philips is due to testify Wednesday next week, the 7th of November. Given the urgency of the matter the -- would the Defence be ready to indicate its position on this motion and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can give a response on this issue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Preferably not close of business, but if somewhere during the day, that will allow us to further look at it. Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivetic will continue his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take up with paragraph 128 of your amalgamated statement which will be P421, and it will be page 29 in the English, page 32 in the B/C/S. And just a point of clarification. In this paragraph, sir, which is not hopefully up on the screen, you describe the use of mobile mortars as a "relatively frequent occurrence." First of all, are you talking here exclusively of the Bosnian Muslim or Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph was that, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Should be the first line.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the reference to the PTT building indicates that I was referring to the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that everything since the heading is Bosnian government mobile mortars that it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within paragraph 128, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 125 which is earlier on the page, you describe the Serb response was sometimes overkill. But would you agree that if a combatant persistently fires upon a party with mobile mortars from a location that that party is entitled respond with counter-fire to neutralize the source?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, yes, but, of course, the fact that it's a mobile mortar means that it is probably well gone by the time the response occurs. So it is that timeline that we're discussing, not the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that such counter-fire in order to be most effective would need to be undertaken as soon as possible after the incoming fire is experienced.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in that instances would you consider it plausible or reasonable that a local artillery commander would have a level of autonomy to be able to respond on his own to such attack without seeking approval of superior commanders for that particular target?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be a disconnect in the statement, because you're assuming that the person who's retaliating is on the scene, but they're not. So they probably won't have a visual on the target that they're trying to engage. So I'm not sure I understand the question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to once fire is determined to have come from a particular direction, return fire can be initiated -- kept by a certain calculations to determine the source of that incoming round. Am I accurate? Approximate location.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One assumes that should the target be an unidentified it would then be sent back to the weapon position and the weapons position would then respond. But they might not have visual contact with the actual target. So there is -- your statement, therefore, doesn't quite make sense. Because, yes, they would be responding of their own initiative, but through a chain of command and through a series of events, which is not the one-to-one event that perhaps you were trying to describe to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. My focus was that that all would happen within the local level of that particular battery that would be responding.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could do. Depending where they had the observation points that were looking and seeking for the targets. Of course, we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. I'd like to ask you to comment upon the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- could I try to better understand the testimony because there seems to be a bit of a -- of a -- apparently you are not using language which the witness grabs as making sense at this moment. Now, I'm trying to understand the situation. A round is fired from within the city by a mobile mortar to, wherever, outside Serbian-held territory. Now, I can understand that if you target a firing position on the Serb side that they see incoming round and they want to respond if they can see where it came from. But I also can imagine that a round is fired which ends somewhere at a distance of 1 kilometre, 500 metres, 2 kilometres from a firing position. Now who would then respond to that incoming fire if you have 5, 6, or 7 positions from where you could respond to that fire? It's not entirely clear to me if you said, A one-to-one position it looks as if from a mobile mortar you fire at a Serbian fire position and then they return that; whereas, that seems to be rather unrealistic. Is that what keeps you apart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was exactly the point I'm making. This is not a one-to-one engagement. Can we have a scenario: Let's say, for example, I mention it in my statement about mobile mortars in a location - doesn't matter where it is - if they fire those weapons, the other side are looking obviously for military targets, they perceive that as a military target because it's engaged them, but the who looks to see what that target is, in my parlance would be a forward observation officer. He would have good vision of the area of conflict. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be necessary, first of all, to decide which firing positions from the Serb side would respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, sir. Because the forward observation officer operates to all the guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So he would pass the information back to a control centre, who would then, with that information, select the weapons to engage the enemy and would give them the details of that and then the engagement would take place. So the people on the weapon site on the Serb side wouldn't necessarily have visual with who they're engaging, obviously by virtue of the range of the weapon. Does that make that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that the mobile mortar may have moved [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another issue, yes. Please proceed. I think I understand what the discussion was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Colonel, for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to these mobile mortars would you be able to make any comment as to their -- how precise or accurate they were compared to regular mortars in the manner that they're being used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a mortar is a mortar. Doesn't matter if it's on the back of a vehicle. It depends on the operator and how effective he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in this respect, perhaps technical. The fact that a mortar is mobile and therefore perhaps installed on a vehicle, that vehicle might be more subject to movement when firing than a mortar which is installed on firm ground. Does that also make no difference at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One would have to reset the weapon after each round, because of that movement that you're suggesting. But even if it was bedded in on the ground, there is inherently a movement anyway. They -- by virtue of them being the indirect fire weapon they are, they are not hugely accurate. They are a significant area weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that these mobile mortars being used by the Bosnian Presidency forces in the manner -- in this manner from vehicles could result in short rounds falling within their own territory instead of on enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's distinctly possible. It is up to the efficiency of the operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me that for purposes of the UNMO statistics any such short rounds coming from these mobile mortars would be indistinguishable from the increp that you would attribute to unmonitored Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't forget that we had people on both sides so that we were always trying to connect outgoing rounds to incoming rounds, so taking that into account, your point is well made. It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's why I said unmonitored --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to call up 1D387 again. That would be your statement from 1997. And this time I'd like to focus on page 12 in the English, page 10 in the B/C/S. And if we could focus on the first full paragraph. We're talking about Sarajevo. I'd like to focus on the third sentence onward of this where you say: "This meant that on the one side the Bosnian Serbs would -- could put pressure on the Presidency in an attempt to control their actions, and on the other side that the Presidency side used Sarajevo to perpetuate their 'victim status' even if they caused the perpetuation. For example, I am aware that on a regular basis, the Presidency forces would employ weapons within the vicinity of Kosevo hospital. In my mind, the Bosnians were on such occasions responsible for bringing fire down upon the hospital. I also know that the Presidency forces could sometimes drive one of their tanks around in the same vicinity. This, I felt, was a direct provocation to the Serbs to shoot at it." First of all, sir, these words that I have read out from your statement, are they truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We talked about, I think, the other incident. I'd like to focus on the tank for the time being and if you could clarify. With the tank being an obviously more visible military target than these soft-skinned civilian mobile mortars, would you expect that it could be target of legitimate incoming fire even if that tank had not fired any rounds?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me -- this statement is referencing Kosevo hospital but would you agree with me that the Presidency forces also utilised mobile mortars from near the PTT building, other hospitals and other humanitarian buildings, including UN installations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that at least on some occasions you and/or perhaps others in the UN structure in Sarajevo asked for these Presidency forces to please move their weapons from near these UN installations before engaging the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I recall correctly, I think the request may have been to place their artillery pieces at least 500 metres from such installations. Am I accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact distance, but we would certainly be insistent to move them with -- so that collateral damage couldn't occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to discuss a different topic. First of all, with regard to the Presidency forces in the Sarajevo area, do you recall that to be the 1st Corps of that army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that approximately half of the 70.000 members of that 1st Corps were located within the inner city itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you define inner city for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Papa zone.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Within the city.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the roughly 30- to 35.000 members of the 1st Corps located within the Papa side of the confrontation line would be legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the UNMO mission have information that such members of the 1st Corps in the Papa side were locating themselves in schools or other civilian type buildings in order to evade being identified as targets by the VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 129 of your amalgamated statement, that would be P421, and this is again page 29 in the English, page 32 in the B/C/S, and while we wait for that, sir, perhaps I can remind you, there you talk about there being a conflict between some elements of the Presidency forces. And as you will see, you give the example of a Juka and again it's paragraph 129. And, first off, I want to ask you when you say conflict, do you actually mean that the so-called Presidency forces or factions thereof engaged in combat with one another?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the expression conflict there would be one of policy and command, not necessarily direct conflict in the combative sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify who this Juka was, am I correct that this was Juka Prazina a local hood or criminal who became propelled to a position as a local military commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- pardon me. If we can now turn to 1D391, which is the transcript of some of your testimony from the Karadzic proceedings, and page 6 in e-court of that document is transcript page 5885 where you were asked a question about the Muslim side --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document D86. And it has only three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. I apologise. I think it's 390. And it should be page 6. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here -- well, let me just present to you the question and the answer as you phrased it: "Q. Would you agree that the Muslim side targeted their own side of the city, that there were shells directed at their own neighbourhoods, their own citizens with the aim of causing them to be perceived as victims and thus inviting international sympathy, compassion and, of course, the military" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be shown on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's line 15 and further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you indicate the line, it's easier for the usher to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Q. ... and, of course, the military intervention that you mentioned. "A. You raise a very good but controversial issue here. I've already in my testimony tried to explain that when incidents are investigated, because we were not in a cease-fire situation but were still engaged in a war, full forensic analysis of all incidents, such as those you've already seen on the incident reports which we discussed yesterday, are such that individual assessment was impossible. On top," and then we have to go to the next page at line 1, "... on top of what I've just said, there was suggestion and there was sufficient unknowns for members of UNPROFOR to be reasonably sure that what you have stated is true. I would not, because of what I've just said, be able to tell you of specific incidences because I would deny anybody in the environment which we lived to have the ability to conclude a satisfactory forensic investigation to prove whether what you have suggested was true or not. So all I can suggest to you was that we, as UNMOs, were uncomfortable about that question because we sensed that what you say may have been true. But there are a lot of riders to what I've just said. It can't be determined that it's a fact, but there are very strong suspicions." And, sir, this portion of the testimony, do you confirm it to be accurate and truthful as to this topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And have I presented the entirety of your comments on this question; that is to say, the riders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to move on to a new topic, and I propose to go through some Sarajevo-Romanija Corps reports with you. First, I would like to call up 1D149. And as we wait for the document, I'll preface my question by indicating that it is dated the 1st December, 1992, and is titled to be a report from -- from Colonel Galic to the Main Staff of the VRS and I'd like to focus on the first paragraph, if we can, which discusses heavily artillery fire coming on the Serb forces from the Presidency forces at Igman, Ctes and Kovaci. First of all, we've discussed Igman, but did UNMO have information about Presidency artillery attacks from these other two locations Ctes and Kovaci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of fire coming into the Serb-controlled areas from other regions. The names of the specific locations, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 2 of this document, there's talk of a successful counter-attack. Would it be reasonable for such a counter-attack to have included counter-fire from artillery or other heavy weapons at these outside regions that you have mentioned and that this document mentions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect a response, a military response from a side that was so engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be reasonable for a military commander having received such a report to conclude that munitions replenishment requests from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were to replenish stocks depleted as a result of the counter-fire used in the counter-offensive against the Presidency forces that had attacked on the 1st of December, 1992, from Igman, Ctes and Kovaci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think just yesterday I mentioned that the resupply during that period would obvious be significantly enhanced to support the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you consider, generally speaking, that such counter-fire could be considered militarily justified or legitimate by a trained military commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to introduce this document as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D149 becomes Exhibit D87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D87 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to 1D129 and the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is another report from Colonel Galic to the VRS Main Staff and it is dated the 4th of December, 1992, a time-period when you were still in the Sarajevo sector. And --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. We don't have English translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way the Prosecution could assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that we noticed this yesterday and we pulled it. I'm just looking for it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could also skip this one and come back to it. That would perhaps be the most efficient use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps meanwhile the Prosecution further seeks to assist you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I do have the English translation that I pulled this morning. It doesn't have an accompanying ERN but I can hand it to the Chamber if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would -- if it would be [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be copied and then at a later moment you use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it first be copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on then for the time being to the next document, which would be 1D130, which -- 1D130 should be dated the 5th of December. I see we still have the prior document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. We don't have this document, as well as English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, I had both of these. I've handed them both to the - thank you - court usher for copying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that the original is not there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the original is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The original is. Okay, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can try 1D131. I'm sounding like a broken record. But hopefully we'll get one that works.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Same, Your Honours. And it seems that they are not released.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suspect that as much, and I'm trying to get word of that to the back but I'm not getting a response yet. Well, let's move ahead then to a document that I know is in the system. Let's -- to deal with this document we'll need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can we try -- let's try 1D130 and see if that one has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that copies are available of 1D129 and 1D130 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if not uploaded, but at least we have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems it is now uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is uploaded. And we can use it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again as we wait for the English to come up, this particular document is dated the 5th of December, 1992, and is dated to be from Colonel Galic to the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it is 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 130, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I started with this one because this one was the first one they told me should be in the system, so going out of order somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And appears to be a combat report for that time-period. If we look at paragraph 1 which describes the enemy forces and there it says that 50 artillery shells were fired upon the Serb forces, and if you look at the third item number it says at 1335 hours 30 shells from 122-millimetre Howitzer were fired from the Brijesce Brdo sector into the Vogosca and Ilidza sectors. The next line says at 1215 hours another attack on Orlic began using gas-filled artillery shells. And the next line, from the Kovaci sector mortar and infantry fire was opened on Vojkovici. First of all, sir, Brijesce Brdo, would you agree that this was another high point outside of Sarajevo that was controlled by the Presidency forces and which was not monitored by the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that comment I can tell you that we did not monitor that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see here a reference to poison gas filled artillery shells allegedly being used against the Serb forces. Did UNMO receive complaints or ever verify that any such armaments were being used by the BiH Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be reasonable to assume that the VRS Sarajevo-Romanija Corps responded to such attacks with artillery counter-fire directed on the forces in Brijesce Brdo and Kovaci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. We didn't monitor it. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider, generally speaking, that such counter-fire could be considered militarily justified or legitimate by a trained military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Ivetic kindly slow down and repeat his previous question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider, generally speaking, such counter-fire could be considered militarily justified or legitimate by a trained military commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, would that be irrespective of what that counter-fire would be, would -- if an atomic bomb would be -- well, of course, this is not to be taken seriously but would it be conditioned in any way whether it would be militarily justified or legitimate apart from whether legitimate is the same as militarily justified. You gave a simple yes as an answer. Do I understand that whatever the counter-fire was, it was always militarily justified or legitimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave a yes answer because yesterday I was asked to keep my answers brief. We're speaking about something that I wasn't present at, that my observers didn't observe, about weapons which we were never had reported to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But "it depends" would be a brief answer as well. If that is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. This is war. It means nothing to answer the question intelligently, quietly in a courtroom about such an issue when there are so many other issues that need to be discussed. It depends how long we can sit here and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let me -- let me be clear. Mr. Ivetic asks you a question whether, generally speaking, such counter-fire, of which you say you have got no idea what it was, could be considered -- you can say, You can always consider something to be justified or legitimate, you always can do that by a trained military commander. So the question, if you wanted to say, Yes, you can do that, but it depends on how it was fired, what was fired, where it was fired. Then the yes is still, I think, the short and accurate answer, because you could do it. Now, of course, this Chamber is not interested in what one could do but is mainly interested in how you should consider that. Now if you say, Without facts, I can't answer that question. That's an answer as well. I'm justifying to find out how we can receive answers which assist the Chamber in its task. And that's the reason why I'm focussing on this matter [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would expect -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, one of the problems that arises here is that there is a lot of hypothesis in your questions, which leads to these kind of discussions. This is a witness of fact. Could we keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. And the witness has testified as to certain conclusions that he believes that a military commander should have had based upon -- asks for -- for a request for replenishment of ammunition. And I'm trying to demonstrate that there are whole other scenarios that are not covered in the witness statement which could be other reasonably understood reasons for replenishment of munitions and asking if they're reasonable. These are the reports that would have been sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I focussed on the question you have put here, and the Chamber sends as a message to you that the hypothetical character of it is strong and that a witness of fact may have difficulties in answering such a question and that's what we established for a fact a minute ago. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will. And I will try to focus my questions more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would it be reasonable for a military commander receiving such a report as this one to conclude that ammunitions replenishment requests from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would be to replenish stocks depleted as a result of this counter-fire against the Presidency forces in Brijesce Brdo and Kovaci?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be clear. Is there anything about return fire, the quantity of that which would, I think, be very important to know before you can ask any question about replenishment of ammunition? Is there anything in this report? Let's first try to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... the report as we've seen -- yes. Counter- fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can -- if we can [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of course replenishment has got something to do with quantities, or am I wrong? I mean, if you fire one shell in return, the need for replenishment might be less than if you fire 10.000 rounds in return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Engagement itself is not significant. It's the quantities, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if there was anything found in this document, then we have, I would say, a factual basis for any further assessment of what a reasonable commander could or should do. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at item 2 where there is the action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay let's look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The way these reports are done, the first item, 1, is always actions; the enemy course is -- item 2 is actions of the friendly forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let's then not talking simultaneously. Let's then take the facts first and then see whether that gives a basis for the question you would like to put to the witness. So we now moved from page 1 to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Item 2. There's only one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Item 2. Let me have a look. I think there is a second page in English. We are there, yes. Item 2. Okay. Let's put -- Please put your questions to the witness so as to establish a basis for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In item 2 we see that the Ilidza Brigade in co-ordination with the Igman Brigade successful carried out an operation Otes and the 1st Sarajevo Brigade is carrying out operations in the direction of Trnovo, as planned, and the other units are firmly holding their previous sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge of the time-period and in particular the operation in Otes, would you agree that there was artillery fire utilised by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that would have required replenishment of their stocks in relation to this combat that is reflected in this report sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let first try to take it step by step. Mr. Mole, your knowledge of what happened on this day in this context, is that -- do you have any recollection of it personally? Or is it on the basis of this document that you have to find a basis for any answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paragraph 2 in particular which relates to the Otes operation I have, as you will have seen from previous testimonies, I have knowledge of that element of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not studied all the previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have your statement [Overlapping speakers] ... Was artillery used at this point in time in the context of this operation? The report is of the 5th of December. And it describes -- it's a regular combat report at 1400 hours on that date. Could you tell us anything about the use and the intensity of the use of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I clarify, are we talking about Otes operation here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about what happened on the 5th of December and what the situation was at 2.00 in the afternoon, not the whole of the Otes operation. Perhaps if -- later, Mr. Ivetic, if you would have questions related to the whole of the Otes operation. But we are at this moment looking at this document, and Mr. Ivetic phrases his questions on the basis, at this moment, of paragraph 2 of this document and, therefore, I'm inquiring what your personal knowledge about this is at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The period, the 2nd of December through to the 7th of December, which includes this date, was, in my understanding, part of an operation called Operation Envelope. It was mounted by the Serb side in response to Presidency attacks on a number of fronts, and the engagement at Otes, yes, it involved significant artillery engagements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So apart from the document, you say not on the basis of it but that your recollection for those days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically Otes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be reasonable for a military commander receiving such a report from this time-period to conclude that munitions replenishment requests from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps artillery were to replenish stocks depleted as a result of this specified activity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what happens now, Mr. Ivetic, is I more or less provided you with a basis for the use of artillery fire but the report doesn't say anything about the intensity of it. And now you focussed the question again on -- on -- on this report which doesn't say anything about artillery ammunition used for artillery fire. I could imagine that you ask the witness, On the basis of your knowledge what you knew if that would be reported, would a reasonable commander under those circumstances take care that replenishment would be there. And then we make it apart from a document which doesn't say anything about it, but it's -- at the same time, it's covering this time-period of early December. Do you understand my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. I thought I asked the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Might have been for the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- receiving such a report. But you apparently wanted to say, Receiving reports containing the information as we just learned you had at the time. Because such reports do not say anything about artillery. The uses of artillery ammunition. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no reports talking about replenishment yet we have the conclusions of this witness going one way about replenishment, so I'm a little bit confused how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed as you wish. But I think I've explained sufficiently what we understand the -- this document can give as assistance and what the information the witness just gave us could assist in further exploring the need for replenishment of artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based on your experiences including your military experience and your experience as the SMO in Sector Sarajevo during this time-period, would you expect that there would have been a need for replenishment of stocks depleted by artillery action in these engagements that we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no experience of anything other than that in the first line relating to Otes. I have indicated in statements previously the numbers of artillery rounds that we were able to verify had been fired into that location and over the period of 2nd to the 7th of December. And that, just to remind you, it was somewhere in the region of 1600 rounds during daylight hours. It was estimated at probably double that over a 24-hour period for the full period, 2nd to the 7th of December. I would obviously expect the weapons that had fired those rounds into that location to be resupplied, to put them back to the stocks that they were at before they began the engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this area, Otes, would that be within the area that you previously defined as being the front lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precisely. The front line went to the west of the village of Otes, and the taking of the village of Otes, of course, went beyond the front line. That's what taking a village would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in that area, there were Bosnian Presidency forces I presume, fighting back. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And those forces fighting back and in the context of that operation that region would have been appropriate for a military target. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree, based upon this document, that there were potential other engagements of which the UNMOs would not have had any information but which could also serve as an explanation for any replenishment requested by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from their superiors?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that question as extremely -- calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't fully understand the question. Mr. Ivetic, would you rephrase it and perhaps split it up, because based upon this document that there were potential other engagement, what do you mean by based on this, upon this document--

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to say there was something beyond this document [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if the witness limited his knowledge to item number 1 of the -- of the section 2. So I presume that means that he is not familiar with the engagements in the direction of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then put to him clearly based on this document, say, may it -- is it possible that beyond what is described here that you may have missed information about other -- be concrete, please. I'm not going to phrase the question for you. These are your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, sir. And presume we're still going on we had decided -- the longer sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we take the shorter sessions. That is agreed upon. Then perhaps you have 20 minutes to think about how to phrase your questions, Mr. Ivetic. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe we were still dealing with this document that's on the screen, which should be, I believe, 1D130. And if I can ask to direct your attention to the item we have been looking at, number 2, would you agree with me that based on this document what is represented here as to Trnovo that at least on this date there was an operation or engagement in an area that would not have been known to the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- now, can we have this document, then, introduced into evidence as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D130 becomes Exhibit D89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to P421 and paragraph 63 of the same. This is the amalgamated statement of the witness. And it's page 15 in English, and I believe it is page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd like to keep in mind the last several lines or -- or sentences of this paragraph of your amalgamated statement in regards to the documents we've just looked at and the documents that we will be looking at for the remainder of the questioning, and I will quote for you, sir: "If ammunition was being replaced on a daily basis, it must be going somewhere. So the question begs: Where was it going? As a commander, I would hope to know where it was going. In this sense, fire missions cannot occur on their own without some kind of accountability, at the minimum through expenditure of ammunition, which the commander would be aware of." Now, sir, in the context of what we've seen at least in the two documents that we've looked at now, would you permit that a commander receiving those specific reports would have an answer for where the ammunition was going and that it would be that it was going towards these other areas outside of the Papa zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly an army commander is dealing with a theatre. You have introduced other aspects of that theatre. My concentration was on Sarajevo and the weapons that we monitored directly pointing at and targeting that city. Weapons, of course, can be moved and target different parts of the same area within range, and we have indicated that the weapons that we monitored sometimes engaged some of the targets that you have just been outlining. Of course, if we're monitoring the firing of those weapons, we're also monitoring the resupply of those weapons. Now, we were not in a position to monitor the resupply of weapons outside of our area of observation, so many of the weapons, which will have engaged the targets that you suggested, could just as easily -- weapons which we weren't monitoring as those that we were. But those that we were, we have an idea of where they fired to, because they are in the shootreps, which we've indicated. So an army commander has to balance the theatre, ammunition expenditure, he and his staff. He would have an expectation of how much ammunition it would require to fulfil his objectives. An army commander who commands throughout Bosnia would treat Sarajevo as but one sector of his responsibility. He would be familiar by reportings, which we've already seen, how much ammunition was being expended to fulfil the task he has given to his subcommander. And I, in my statements, indicated that the numbers of rounds required to fulfil the task of containment of Sarajevo seemed to be at variance to the task. In my understanding, from our comprehension of the front line round Sarajevo, the lack of that variation on that front line through that three-month period, there were -- there was more ammunition expenditure within that period than one would expect to contain the city militarily. That is the point I'm making.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And just to be clear, in paragraph 63, the commander you're talking about is identified as Commander Galic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "any commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But the -- the paragraph 63 talks about: "Giving Galic's dependancy on artillery it would have been essential for him to essentially -- to carefully monitor the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the battle around and the takeover the Otes that we discussed would have been a change in the front lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to 1D131 in e-court, dated the 5th of December, 1992. And hopefully -- hopefully both versions are in e-court. And this is a report from Colonel Galic to the VRS Main Staff. And if we could focus on paragraph 1 which would be the recitation of the enemy activity. And we see here that is says: "In the afternoon the enemy continued persistent attacks on Orlic and Zuc and succeeded in pushing back the forces of the Vogosca Brigade by 700 metres in the Orlic area." And then if we could look at the last line: "During the whole day, the enemy opened strong artillery fire on the whole zone of the corps." And we see also there: "Attacks continued from Ormanje and Igman towards Hadzici." First of all, is Ormanje another Presidency heavy -- heavy weapon site that was outside of Sarajevo and thus unmonitored by the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was unmonitored by the UNMO mission, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the Orlic and Zuc areas, are you familiar with a BH Presidency force offensive that, in fact, captured and took over this region during the time-period that you were at the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll very familiar with Zuc, having gone up there and visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that be a change in the situation as we discussed before, a change in [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map which I drew in the early days you'll recall, if you've seen it, has a dotted line across Zuc and that was because it was an area that went backwards and forwards in terms of possession for either side throughout the period. And if I might, I'll just make the connection here, that I perhaps corrected you earlier on in terms of fire going to places that you weren't necessarily sure, and you were suggesting that it was a Serb province as opposed to Presidency. I'll make it clear now that the Presidency forces within Sarajevo city fired in support of their forces at Zuc and that was the rationale for my commenting earlier on that it was not just a Serb feature firing onto Igman as opposed to firing upon into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. And with regard to this document, if we can look at item number 2 and we see here that: "Despite strong enemy resistance the Ilidza Brigade in co-operation with the Igman Brigade is successfully operating in Otes - two thirds of Otes had been liberated." Can we confirm that this would be the same Otes operation that you previously testified to have knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited by one of my colleagues to slow down, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise and thank you for the advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph of item 2 says that the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade is conducting operations towards Trnovo. First of all, a mechanised brigade would be heavy weapons. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appreciating that all organisations under different militaries have different compositions, but the premise of a brigade is it's the first level of command where you'll get all arms involved in one unit. I'm sorry. That's rather a long answer to a straightforward question, but you would expect artillery within the brigade and under command of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, the location of this engagement towards Trnovo, I believe you've already identified that was not a combat engagement that you or the UNMO mission were monitoring or were familiar with; is that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of this report would a commander receiving this report be able to understand and answer the question of where munitions were going? Would he be looking at these specific engagements as rationale for replenishment of munitions to this particular subordinate unit, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in your --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a principle, yes. But the quantities we've already discussed are not something that we could identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. And again, the quantities are not listed here, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have this introduced as the next available exhibit number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D131 becomes Exhibit D90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to 1D132 in e-court. This is another report from Colonel Galic of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the VRS Main Staff. This one dated the 6th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, again, in the first paragraph we have the enemy action where it is reported that from 200 hours the enemy continually fired 105-millimetre and 102 [sic] millimetre shells and VBR multiple rocket-launcher missiles at Ilidza, Hadzici, Zunovicna, Ilinjaca, Dobrinja, Nedzarici and Vojkovici. From Malo Polje, Veliko Polje and Hrasnici and that over 200 missiles were fire. First of all, sir, I believe, Malo Polje and Veliko Polje are the Igman location that we've previously discussed, and we have had Hrasnici, I think, in a previous document. Would you agree that these are all sites that the UNMO was not in a position to monitor, these BH Presidency artillery locations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And just to make the matter totally clear that if weapons such as that had been available to the Presidency forces within Sarajevo, then, clearly, we would have been monitoring them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at item number 2 on this document which indicates the action of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and states that: "Our artillery pounded at the firing positions of enemy artillery at Igman and at Hrasnici and also fire at infantry in Sokolovic Kolonja, Buca Potek and Boljakov Potok." Are these combat engagements that you had any knowledge of as part of the UNMO mission or would they be outside of the remit of the UNMO -- of -- not the mission but outside the remit the facts that you had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and [indiscernible] shot, the firing of the weapons or the monitoring had been executed as part of the UNMO mission and you know what that was, then clearly these were outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And then again, a senior commander receiving such a report would answer your question posed of where the ammo -- could answer the question of where the ammo is going in relation to this particular combat. Would that be, generally speaking, a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be a relationship between that report he has received and the presumable ammunition resupply requests he'd receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly the correct answer that I was looking for. I apologise for not being able to correctly ask the question. With -- with regard to -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess -- I tendered this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D132 becomes Exhibit D91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, yesterday we received an indication of one hour 15, one hour 20. We went already beyond the one hour 20, I think. Could you give us an indication as how much more time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have just one or two more documents, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 1D325.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this, sir, is dated the 23rd of December, 1992, so it would have been near the end of your tour of duty at the UNMO Sector Sarajevo. Again, it is a report of Colonel Galic reporting to the Main Staff of the VRS. And once the English comes up if we could focus on the first paragraph to begin. And we'll see here that the enemy artillery is reported of engaging in fierce offensive activity in the north western sector of the front. And we see here various amounts of shells being shot into Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca and Ilijas. And there's indication there that says: "Which is an indication that the enemy has received larger quantities of ammunition of all calibre, since they fired from all the artillery weapons at their disposal." And I would ask you, sir, first of all, do you recall, based upon your information, if there was a time-period when even the artillery within the Papa zone of the Presidency side was able to have more ammunition than in previous months when your testimony was that it had -- that it had -- minimal amount of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to clarify that question. Are you asking was the Presidency side within the city now reinforced with additional ammunition, as a result of this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking whether you had any knowledge of them being reinforced with additional munitions, you being the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They being within the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Within the city, correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, there is no doubt that they could not have continued with the -- and maintained their resistance to the siege situation unless they had had access to additional ammunition, which, of course, we had no direct knowledge of. But I'm not too sure how you relate this answer to the question about the enemy artillery opening fire from the following areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was more concerned about the time-period. Did you note that near the end of your tour of duty that the Bosnian Presidency forces within the Papa zone appeared to have more ammunition available for their heavy weapons than they did at the beginning of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly did. And they also had additional weapons. Of that we're quite sure. We wouldn't document that but we are pretty sure that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear you say additional weapons, do we mean heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: More medium weapons, I would suggest. If one takes a tank as a heavy weapon, major artillery piece is a heavy weapon, not so. But more mortars, yes, of the higher calibre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if we can look at item number 2 on this document, it starts of by saying that: "All SRK units are in full B/G combat readiness. They are repulsing the enemy attacks successfully." And would, therefore, a commander -- well, first of all, do you have knowledge of these attacks that were occurring on the 23rd of December on these regions, Hadzicic, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca, Ilijas by artillery bombardment by the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were very familiar with what was occurring within the region of Sarajevo. You'll recall that earlier in my testimony I related the fact we had operations group meetings in the morning, and information such as this would be made available to the sector and therefore to the United Nations Military Observers. So we always tried to place into context what was occurring on in direct area of Sarajevo the city with what happened in the region. And this example that you're pointing out to me now was part of a significant Presidency offensive on a number of fronts. This identifies that offensive and it identifies the response to it, of which Otes was another response to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, to tie this to the question that you posed in paragraph 63 of your amalgamated statement, would a commander receiving reports of such significant actions have at least one answer for where the ammunition was going in terms of those particular engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And just to supplement my yes, we, as UNMOs, would be fully appreciative of the expenditure of ammunitions on these supernumerary tasks, if one could not make that comment sound too trite, but supernumerary military tasks that were occurring outside our immediate area of responsibility. So our awareness of them tells you that we would account for them in terms of expected ammunition expenditure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can ask for this document to be accepted into evidence as the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D325 becomes Exhibit D92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you for your time and your detail to answer my questions. You've helped me understand your testimony a lot.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, any need -- yesterday you said about four questions. Has that grown during the night?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, well, not during the night but it has grown in the last session. I would -- also I can, whenever the Court suggests that I do it, address the matters of the evidence that was MFI'd, that we left MFI'd yesterday. I can do that at the conclusion of the witness's testimony or now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to conclude the evidence of the witness and then deal with these administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, first I would just like to turn your attention to the subject matter of the mobile mortars that was discussed with you during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if we could have on the screen, please, the witness's statement, which is P421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which paragraph on which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And it would be paragraph 126, Your Honours, which is at page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the hard copy page, yes, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And, Colonel, do you have it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I would draw your attention to the portion of that paragraph where -- again regarding mobile mortars, where you write, "When the Serbs fired in response" -- I'm sorry. Beginning at the sentence above: "If a professional operator targets something, you can expect a concentration of fire in that area. When the Serbs fired in response, there was no such concentration of fire because the mortar had gone. This was therefore retaliation rather than a military response." Can you explain to us what you're talking about there in terms of the concentration of fire that you would expect to see and what your own observations were of what you saw of Serb responses -- military response to mobile mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When engaging a target such as you've pointed out to me, the mobile mortar, it's a matter of timeline and proportionality. Sometimes it's also a matter of what weapon you use to engage the enemy as to how effective that would be. Let me take that point first. Earlier on, we were talking about the possibility of a lone tank moving somewhere close to a sensitive area, such as a hospital, to draw fire, and I stated that that happened. The response to that by firing artillery rounds at a tank isn't necessarily the best response. It's not appropriate because an indirect fire weapon of the accuracy we're talking of is unlikely to be effective against that particular weapon, a tank. You would want to take that tank out by another direct fire, i.e., an anti-tank round or a tank. So the first part of engaging one of these targets is decision of what you're going to use to engage it, the quantity, therefore, its proportionality, and then the timeline. So now we move maybe to the mobile mortars. The very fact that they are mobile, the very fact that they were located proximatus to a sensitive area means that one's response has to accord with the target. We've already discussed that there is a passing of time, crucial time, between identifying that target, let's say, a forward observation officer identifies the mobile mortars firing from its firing location, reports that fact back to his commander. His commander would then presumably allocate the weapons to return the fire, and by the time that detail is passed to the heavy weapon operator and the target is engaged, obviously the weapon that you're originally engaging, the mortars, could and probably have moved. So that's the timeline. And then one has to consider what sort of response it is that you are giving to the initial engagement. If there are a lot of rounds fired at a place that the enemy is no longer at, not only is that a waste of ammunition, but it is also, of course, likely to cause casualties beyond what your original target was. Those are all the considerations that one would take into account when considering an engagement such as you described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question in this context. A mobile mortar fires and the time it needs to respond to that fire is such that the mobile mortar most likely will have left the location from where it fired, which leaves you almost empty handed because either you fire at the larger region where the mortar initially was, which you say is not an appropriate way of doing, if I understand you well, which means that you would be left behind with frustration and no legitimate answer. Is that -- well, at least more or less what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's war, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I would just like to understand if you criticise the answer given, the response given by the attacked party, that there is no -- whatever you do, it's always wrong. You would agree with that? Apart from lodging complaints and -- I mean, but militarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's extremely frustrating and what you're dealing with are two totally different weapons systems and it's sledge hammer to crack a nut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, is -- just in terms of -- in terms of the -- a legitimate response to a -- to a mobile mortar in that situation, would an attack on another military target in response also be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that from, say, the Serb side, that by not being able to engage the original target, they might engage another?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: For example.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's -- is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Yes. They might well do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yesterday -- I'm moving on from that topic. Yesterday at transcript page 70 to 71, you -- you agreed, and I'm paraphrasing here that the incident forms that we've discussed in the course of your testimony that your UNMOs used could also include outgoing fire. So could -- sorry. Your incident forms recorded fire on those incident forms could also include outgoing fire from Serb artillery directed at Mount Igman rather than at the Papa zone. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Obviously if an increp is being completed appropriately then the fact that the weapon fires means that you would continue the completion of the serial on the increp by filling out that information that you're just suggesting, i.e., what was the proposed target.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, just so -- so I understand you, it would be a shootrep?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... then not an increp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're monitoring the weapon and the weapon happens to be firing at a different target than what you expected, it's still a shootrep and it would be recorded as to what the expected target was, assuming that the UN Military Observer asked the commander the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And so taking that into account, does -- does that in any way affect your observations, the possibility that -- that these shootreps could have -- could also include outgoing fire from Serb artillery directed at Igman, although the shootreps would have, if done correctly, recorded that. Does that in any way affect your observations about the fire that was being directed from Serb positions into the centre of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the completion of the shootrep would indicate what the expected target was. So we would be familiar with it. We would understand it. We would accord it as part of our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn for a moment to the document -- actually, I'll do that, sorry, at the end because it will require going into private session. So I'll put that question later. Yesterday you testified at page what was page 28 -- I'm sorry today page 28 of the temporary transcript, line 24, to page 29, line 3, you were asked whether those forces fighting back and in the context of that operation that region would have been appropriate for a military target, in the context of, I believe, it was talking about the Otes operation. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked is that accurate. And your answer was, Yes, it was an engagement. And I'd like to just draw your attention to that question and answer and ask you to clarify. In the context of -- even in the context of the military engagement does that make that whole region into an appropriate military target, or are there still tactical decisions to be made about what can be targeted within that region?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just have to be reminded of the region that we were discussing. Can you help there?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we were discussing the region of Otes but just for certainty's sake, I'm going to look. If you'll give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: And this area, Otes, would that be within the area that you previously defined? No, that's the front lines. Let me see... Yes. And those -- so you were talking about the area of Otes: "And those forces fighting back and in the context of that operation," and that was the operation about Otes, "that region would have been appropriate for a military target. Is that accurate? Your answer was: "Yes. It was an engagement."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The engagement in Otes, by virtue of what was going -- what the objective was from the Serb side, was to take the village of Otes and to square off the west hand -- western end of the city to allow communications for themselves on a north/south axis to be easier. The front line originally was obviously to the west of the village of Otes, and that conflict to which you refer became the area of intense artillery fire for the period we've discussed 2 through 7 of December. So of necessity, behind the front line where you would expect conflict then became the front line, by virtue of that conflict. That was the basis of my saying that the area was a military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask, please, for Exhibit P425 up on the screen. And if we could just -- if we could, please, have, I believe, it's the next page, the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, I'm afraid this is going to be a long question. Several of the exhibits that you commented on during the course of the cross-examination, such as D87, 90 and 91, illustrated the confrontation that was going on in the first week of December 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And several of those -- the questions and answers that you gave when commenting on those documents show that BiH forces from Igman, amongst other places, such as Kovaci and Otes were attacking Serb positions. So I'm drawing your attention to that area of the cross-examination. Now, P425 on the screen, which is the December end-of-month report, if we look at the entries for, let's say, the 1st through 4th of December, 1992, which is the same time-period as those reports. We see on the 1st of December 330 rounds recorded into the Presidency -- the Presidency positions -- the Presidency monitoring sites in Sarajevo. UNMOs recorded 330 rounds into the Presidency positions; 264 rounds on 2nd of December; 1284 rounds on the 3rd of December; and 1480 rounds on the 4th of December. Can you explain to us, please, is there any connection or what is the connection, if any, between the confrontation described -- as described in the Defence exhibits in those areas outside of the -- outside of the city of Sarajevo where your UNMOs were located at their Papa positions and what your UNMOs were observing in Sarajevo as shown in this December en- of-month report, P425.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I try and paraphrase the question so that I can answer the right one? But I think, are you asking what the relationship is between the weapons we monitored and what targets they engaged during that period?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, can you answer that question and then I may follow up on your answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this course of this period of intense artillery activity, all the weapons that we were monitoring were engaged in the conflict. The majority of them, should they be in range, fired at Otes and into the region of Otes. That is not to say that some of them didn't fire elsewhere because we know that the range on some was insufficient for purpose to support that engagement. We also know that having seen the evidence that there were other pressure points that the Serbs felt that they were under by virtue of attacks the Presidency were making. Zuc was a good example, and there were others besides around the front line of the city. So other weapons that we were monitoring targeted there. I also state that during the course of that period, there were considerable number of rounds still fired into the city, not on the front line, not into Otes.
