I don't recall ever knowing of or being told or reporting that any of the weapons that we monitored or were aware of fired out of the city at that time; i.e., they concentrated their fire at Otes or the front line or the city. I cannot recall any report - I might be wrong - but I cannot recall any report of any of that fire being directed elsewhere. It was concentrated very much on the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. So can I just ask you to clarify from what you've -- the end of that answer that you've just said: "I don't recall ever knowing or being told that any of the weapons that we monitored or were aware of fired out of the city at that time." Which weapons are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those weapons that we monitor or we were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Inside the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The ones we monitored on Lima side, on Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to see whether we understood as well. What you are actually saying is all those weapons we monitored were focussing either on the conflict on Otes or perhaps Zuc. They were also firing into the city itself. But you're not aware of any engagement to other front lines or other combat areas apart from these at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the numbers that are reflected -- the numbers that are reflected in your December end-of-month report as incoming rounds into the Presidency side, that's referring to -- into the centre of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Into the area of observation from our UN Military Observers without being too pedantic, in principle, yes, inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Finally, Colonel Mole, in terms of -- and I believe you touch on this in your -- in your statement as well. But in terms of what you would expect to see -- what you would expect to see in terms of the locations that were damaged within the city of Sarajevo, for fire that was targeting military -- military targets, can you explain to us what your expectations would be even taking into account that sometimes military targets are missed or mobile, and what the actual damage that you saw was? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Am I allowed a relatively long answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: You can't look at me for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, usually long answers are triggered by -- by questions with some vagueness in it. But please give it a try, as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It's a balance between what is expected from our understanding of the military situation and what we saw. If I might give you an example. If there was a headquarters position within the -- within the city and it's an accepted military target for the Serbs to engage, I would expect a concentrated fire order, a concentrated attack, and consequent damage. Otes says they could do that. We know that they could engage targets effectively. Therefore, one then has to question why we saw - and they are recorded - so many rounds throughout the city not anywhere near targets we knew of. I accept the rider that we didn't know all the targets, but we knew a lot from the sources of information that we had. My own personal experience of driving round the city, walking, was such that I had a free remit to walk and go anywhere I wished. My personal experience of weapons that were being engaged whilst I was walking or driving round the city say to me there were no direct targets of a military nature where those rounds were landing. Excuse me. If I'm driving in the western part of Sarajevo, Novi Grad, there were very few buildings on the road network. Why, then, would there be multiple rounds in a very general area fired into empty space? Space that anybody could be travelling through at any particular time, and, more often than not, my UN Military Observers, or myself, was doing exactly that. There's no perceived target there. What else are we expected to think? We have the analysis which I've tried to explain to the courtroom of where you would expect fire to be at any particular time. To experience that then has to be rationalised. Going back to where the headquarters may be, for example, in the old town on the east of the city, a concentrated fire mission could effectively destroy it. If you are an intelligent person, you would remove the headquarters or remnants of it, if it had been hit, somewhere else, then explain to me why we would get continued rounds going into the old city not in a particularly targeted fashion, not concentrated fire, and over a long period of time. It doesn't make any correlation to the ability that we knew that the Serbs and their artillery had available to them. And it's that mismatch which we're trying to analyse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, I'm looking at the clock. How many --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You concluded your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One question that arises out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll first ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I would have one or two relatively short questions, and I hope relatively short answers as well. Questioned by the Court: Mr. Mole, a number of questions were asked in relation to the number of incoming fire on the Serb side and on the Papa side. Specifically two or three documents were shown to you where the incoming fire on the Serb side was at a higher number than at the Papa side. Does that reflect the overall picture? Was it equal incoming fire? Was there ordinarily, that means more days, more incoming fire on the Papa side? Could you give us any indication where we looked at instances where clearly the incoming fire on the Serb side was of a higher number. The overall picture. Without going into details.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our concentration was very much looking inwards to the city by virtue of the location of the UN Military Observer OPs. When we started, that was very much our focus, but it would be very unfair and unbalanced if we didn't accept that parts of the city were actually occupied by the Serb side rather than the Presidency side, which I'm sure you're probably aware of, but Nedzarici, Ilidza and so on. As a consequence, we have to include them within our observations and it is only appropriate that we do. And as soon as we do that, we see that those places came under intense pressure from artillery fire outside of our immediate area of observation. That's the reason those figures are presented to you, and they are rightly and appropriately interpreted that way. They have come from outside our immediate area of responsibility, but the pressure that the Serb side, or Lima side, felt was very understandable and intense on occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Some questions were put to you in shells falling short although directed outside -- from inside the city to the -- to the Serb positions outside the city. Did you -- that was suggested as a possibility and I think you agreed that such a possibility does exist. Did you ever find incidents where you could establish that a shell fell fired from a direction where you could not but possibly conclude that it fell short of where it should have landed, in terms of direction and in terms of where it fell close to the confrontation lines? Did you -- apart from the theoretical possibility, did you ever find such a thing on the ground or indications, not necessarily conclusive evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, if I'm going to be very brief in the answer, that isn't the case. The only experience that I personally had of such an event was when a tank round hit the room that I was in but fortunately didn't go off. Now you would say, Was that one from the Presidency side that fell short and hit us, or did it come from outside the other side of the confrontation line. That is the difficulty we have in interpreting it. But I think to answer your question that, overall, no, I can't recall ever being aware of a specific incident where that occurred. But it has a possibility, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have testified to that. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Ivetic, I suggest that we take a break after we concluded the testimony of Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreeable, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic:

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, very briefly, at temporary transcript page 50, lines 12 through 17, you were asked by the Prosecution whether the numbers that are reflected in your December end-of-month report as incoming rounds into the Presidency side are referring to -- into the centre of the city of Sarajevo. You answered: "Yes, into the area of observation from our UN Military Observers without being too pedantic, in principal, yes, inside the city." Am I correct that the rounds that were directed towards Otes would have been considered rounds into the zone of observation of UNMO and therefore into the city as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And specifically Papa 5 was the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, for the MFIs from yesterday -- well, let me first doing something else. Mr. Ivetic, I think I fully understand that you do not need to tender 1D00387. That's the statement from Mr. Mole from 1997. I think you have read everything you wanted to. Same would be true for the transcript of the Karadzic case, 18th of August, 2010 and finally also the -- what you read from the transcript in the Galic case, the evidence of Mr. Tucker. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we've dealt with that. Ms. Hochhauser, should the witness be present if we deal with your last --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: There's no need for him to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll first -- Mr. Mole, I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Ivetic and I communicated last night. He proposed to me and we agreed that P430 -- that's currently MFI's as P430 that the whole document would be end into evidence. He has withdrawn any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P430 is therefore now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: As to P431 which is the transcript of the 6th Assembly -- the transcript of the 6th Assembly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: As to P431 which is the transcript for the 16th Assembly, we have agreed that, through Colonel Mole, only the excerpt regarding Mr. Karadzic's statement on a the fifth strategic objective would be entered into evidence through this witness, but I have -- we have a suggestion if it is acceptable to the Court to enter it as P431A and to keep the entire document MFI'd as P431. The reason being, Your Honours, that I believe that others, during the course of the Prosecution case, will refer to portions of the transcript, and -- and we may as well actually at some point offer the entirety the transcript, and it would prevent the record from being littered with little pieces of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the excerpt P431A been uploaded and under what number?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: No. I wanted to wait for Your Honours' permission before doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Chamber grants leave to proceed. So we'll wait until you have uploaded it and then we'll decide on admission, once we have the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Elvir Pasic as the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the witness is being brought in, perhaps I might give a brief explanation of the exhibit that has recently been added to the exhibit list for this witness. That's Exhibit 28487. During the proofing on the 31st of October, 2012, the witness was shown a list of 64 names. These 64 names were taken from an exhumation report from Paklenik pit. That is Prosecution Exhibit P00315 that was on the list for this witness. The witness was also shown an additional name that appears in a separate table on page 8 of this exhibit. That name was provided in the statement of another witness. The witness was given no information about these names by the OTP, and the witness provided comments on the names he recognised in that list together -- and that list, together with the witness's comments were made into a Prosecution exhibit, 65 ter 28487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From the Defence, will it be -- Mr. Stojanovic, will it be you who will examine the witness or cross-examines the witness? Are there any problems in relation to this, and the way in which the Prosecution proceeded here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We have received this and we believe that there will be no problem in using it during the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic. Mr. Pasic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. And, Mr. Jeremy, I hereby inform you that leave is granted to add 65 ter 28487 to the 65 ter list. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: My name is Elvir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, is it true that you have previously provided a written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor and testified before this Tribunal in other trials?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In particular, did you provide a written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated 21 October 2004?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that 65 ter 28434 be brought on our screens. It is a statement of Mr. Pasic dated 21 October 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, it says 1994 on the document that was given to us. Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. It's 1994. That's my error. 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where it is transcribed "2004", we're talking about the statement, 1994. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can I ask you to view the page on the screen before you; and at the bottom of that page, can you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the last page of this statement; e-court page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Pasic, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read and review this statement in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And having read that statement, do you have any changes that you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If I were today to ask you questions similar to those that you were asked in the taking of that statement, would you provide the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: In substance, yes, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders this is statement, 65 ter 28434 as the next Prosecution public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, no objections? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28434 becomes Exhibit P434, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P434 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I'll now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. In 1992, Mr. Pasic was a serving policeman in Rogatica. He describes the takeover of Rogatica and his detention in the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school, the Susica camp and the Batkovic camp. After the takeover the people were told that Rogatica was designated a Serbian municipality and that the Serbs intended to cleanse the town of Muslim extremists. The witness hid in the basement of his apartment block together with a number of other Bosnian Muslims, including his mother and grandmother. On the 7 of June, 1992, the witness and others were captured by men in military fatigues. They separated the Bosnian Muslim men from the women and their hands were tied with wire. The witness, together with Muslim men and women, were then detained in the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school for 20 days. On the 27th of June, 1992, the witness and about 280 others were transferred. En route, the witness and 28 other Muslim men were then separated and detained in an abandoned farm building for 20 days. Thereafter, the witness was transferred to the Susica camp in Vlasenica where he and others were physically abused by the camp commander, Dragan. The following day, the witness was transferred to Batkovic camp where he remained for over a year. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Do you have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to tender the one associated exhibit for this witness, 65 ter 28435. This is a sketch of Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28435 becomes Exhibit P435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also like to place on the record the adjudicated facts on reliance on which the 92 ter statement has been redacted and the reliance on which certain evidence will not be elicited during this examination. They are as follows: 505, 506, 508, 509, 510, 512, 513, 514, 516, 1119, 1120, 1121, 1122, 1125, 1128, 1129, 1132, 1133, 1258, and 1263.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in paragraph 12 of your statement, now in evidence as P434, e-court page 4 in both languages, you state that in late March/early April 1992, you decided to leave the Rogatica police force shortly after it had been separated along ethnic lines. Why did you make the decision to leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for this decision to leave the police, I reached it for a simple reason because the police force in Rogatica was divided in two, of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Republika Srpska. And this led to a single development: Conflict. I personally did not want to be drawn into any kind of conflict, political or armed conflict, so I decided to leave the police force and I returned my uniform, therefore, as well as my weapons, and the ammunition that I had and that I had received as a member of the reserve police force in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of your statement, e-court page 5, you state that on May the 25th, 1992, around mid-day, the conflict broke out in Rogatica. In a few sentences can you tell us when you realised that the town was being attacked?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was in one of the cafes in town with my girlfriend and with my friends. We were playing billiards. All of a sudden we heard strong reverberations, a sound which we could not trace. We ran out to see what was going on, and we realised that the city was being shelled and that shells were falling in the centre of town. We were confused. We didn't know what to do. We tried to hide. We tried to save ourselves, and I decided to save my mother and I went throughout town in order to get home, even though shells were falling. When I got home, my mother was also confused. She didn't know what to do. She started carrying food, putting it into a car that we had. We thought that we would be safer in this big building, but halfway the car broke down so we had to hide in one of the private houses in one of those streets there for a while until the shelling stopped. This lasted for about three or four hours. After that, we managed to go to the building where we had lived basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And had you been given any warning that this attack would start?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. No warning whatsoever. It was totally out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 and 21 of your statement, e-court page 6 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S -- 5 and 6 in the B/C/S, you refer to a JNA armoured personnel carrier entering Rogatica town. Soon after you refer to an announcement being made, stating: "The Serbs intended to cleanse Rogatica of Muslim extremists and so-called Green Berets allegedly consisting of 4.000 people." Mr. Pasic, were you aware of the existence of any of these 4.000 Muslim extremists or Green Berets in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I knew, there weren't any military organisations or extremists in the territory of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And shortly before this time, you were a policeman in Rogatica. If such extremists or Green Berets were active, would you have expected to have been aware of them?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Probably. Because, as a policeman in Rogatica, I noticed columns of the JNA passing through town but I didn't notice any other military formations near town or going through town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: At paragraph 22 of your statement, e-court page 6, you describe hiding in the basement of your apartment building shortly before you were arrested. How many others were hid in the basement with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: About 20 or so people were there in the basement where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And upon your arrest, could you tell us what you could observe when you came out of the basement in a sentence or two?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: When we were thrown out of the basement, what impressed me was the flames around our building. You could feel the smell of houses burning. People were lying on the ground. Faces to the ground, hands on the back. Women were standing in a corner by the building. There were about 20 of them there with children. The shelling of town was still going on, but the intensity was not as high as it had been about half an hour before that when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 22 of your statement you state that the men were: "Masked and uniformed." Can I describe the uniforms of these men?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers that came to take us prisoner in the building and to evict us from the building, they wore camouflage JNA uniforms that were olive green grey. Some of them wore grey-blue camouflage uniforms that I had occasion to see in the police. For the most part their faces were covered with black caps. There were only two of them that did not wear any caps like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you refer to the names of these men in paragraphs 22 and 24 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would note that these names are listed as names 3, 6, 18, and 26 in Exhibit P00313, which I don't wish to call up at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the men who had been separated from the women you have said their hands were behind their back. Were their hands tied?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: At first, when we just got out, we all had to lie on our chests and to face the ground. At that point in time, our hands had not been tied. However, later, I noticed that the men who remained in front of the building were lying there with their hands tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did you observe what their hands were tied with?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Their hands were tied with a wire. It would be easiest for me to describe it in the following way: It looked as if a tire, a car tire had burned and then there are wires left. That's what it looked like. The wires that were used to tie their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement, e-court page 7, you describe being the only man permitted to leave with the group of women that were taken to Veljko Vlahovic school. The other men being taken from the basement remained behind. Aside from one man, Enes Korjenic, whom you refer to in paragraph 26 of your statement, did you ever see any of these men alive again?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your statement, you state that Enes Korjenic told you that a man named Rajko Kusic intervened to release him from this group of men. Who was Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Rajko Kusic was the main commander of the Serb armed forces in the territory of the town of Rogatica. He was an inhabitant of Rogatica before the conflict. He worked in a company there, a factory, and Enes Korjenic worked in the same company. Now whether this affected Rajko Kusic's decision to let Enes Korjenic go back to his family or not, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that 65 ter 28487 be brought to our screens. And this is the list of names that I mentioned at the start of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, while this exhibit is being brought onto the screens during your proofing on the 31st of October, 2012, do you recall being shown a list of 65 names?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you told any information about these names by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall recognising certain of these names and providing comments on the names to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to the last page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you recognise your signature on this last page?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall whether any of the names you recognised and commented on were involved in any military activity in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that any of them was involved in any military activity in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you recognised 16 of these 64 names. Of these 16 names you recognised, you referred to last seeing ten of these persons listed as name 4, 12, 15, 41, 42, 48, 53, 59, 60, and 64. You're listing these names, these men as having their hands tied behind their back with wire. Were these men among the group that you discussed earlier in your testimony today, the group of men with their hands tied behind their back on the ground outside your apartment building on the 7th of June, 1992, who were being guarded by the Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And was one of these men your uncle?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in paragraph 30 of your statement, e-court page 8, you state: "On June 27, we were all picked up with the exception of doctors, engineers, and mechanics." And here you're referring to being picked up from the Veljko Vlahovic school. Was one of the men who remained behind Muho Besilja [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Mujo Besilja, yes. He stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would note that on the last page of 65 ter 28487 Mr. Pasic provides details about the last time he saw Mujo Besilja. At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28487 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence objects to this proposal, simply because we don't think that this is sufficient standard to introduce this document through this witness. First of all, this document is practically a product of the Prosecution, and it is a compilation of statements and lists made by the OTP. By compiling a piece of evidence in that manner and then tendering it into evidence, we don't think satisfies the relevant standard. Secondly, on the basis of footnotes and comments which are an integral part of this document, you can see that there are comments that only testify to the fact that this person was recognised and identified, whereas his subsequent fate is not known. For all these reasons, the Defence is opposed to tendering this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as earlier described, the names were given to this witness. No indication was given to the witness from where they came. The witness has -- this is an exhibit created by this witness in terms of the comments that he provides in respect to the names from this list that he recognises. On that basis, I submit it's relevant and probative and should be accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I did not fully understand your observation that, since the final fate of these persons is not known, is it your position that you cannot ask a witness to recognise people and ask him when you saw them last time without the witness knowing what finally happened? Is that -- would you expect a witness to provide the full evidence until the very end, or could he just give what he knows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer, can we have the document on the screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not analysing at this moment the issue of what happened to these persons. This is not the time to do that. I just want to reiterate that if you look at comments provided by the witness under number 7, for example, there's no other information other than that he knew that person. There is no other information provided as to what happened to this individual. The fact that this is a compilation document, which was practically drawn up by the OTP based on the statement of this witness, we do not see any relevance ground for tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection and admits the document into evidence. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28487 becomes Exhibit P436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P436 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, as a final question, based only on what you could personally observe, as a former policeman responsible for law enforcement within Sanski Most who observed the attack from the inside and later the outside of the town, did that attack appear to you to be an organised and planned attack?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's mention of Sanski Most here. Maybe it's a misinterpretation. Probably the reference was made of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The mistake is mine; forgive me. When I referred to Sanski Most, I meant to refer to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: The attack on Rogatica, as I see it, had been organised and I'm relying on the fact that it was launched exclusively on Muslim populated parts of the town and the attack was launched from nearby villages that were 2 or 3 kilometres from the town, and those villages were mostly populated by Serbs. So, judging by all of that, the attack on town was definitely an organised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly the first statement you gave during the war while you were a refugee in the UK ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of May, 1996, you testified before this Tribunal. Can you remember if that is correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but it was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in any other case after 1996 in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I testified twice, once in Tadic case and the second time in the Nikolic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point, receive summons from the BH Court to testify about your experience relating to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. I had never been summoned by the BH Court to testify about any acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That means neither Susica nor Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. Not by the BH Court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please, a short break between question and answer. And, Mr. Pasic, would you also take a short break after the question, before you answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so, Your Honours. Can we please have in e-court the statement dated 20th October 1994, which is Exhibit P ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P434, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Pasic, that here you speak about the fact that in the period between September 1991 until the end of that year, call-ups for military exercise became pretty regular. Then you say: "The Muslims generally did not respond because it was feared that they would be sent to fight at the front in Croatia. On the other hand, the Serbs tended to comply with the call-ups." What was your experience that prompted you to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: From September 1991 onwards, there was a conflict inside the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, specifically in Croatia and Slovenia. The Yugoslav People's Army started becoming active in those areas and the reserve contingent of the JNA was called up to react in those areas. The Muslim population did not want to go and fight another Yugoslav people. The majority of my friends refused to respond to the call-up and join the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, based on your experience, you made this statement. And also based on the contacts with the people that you had who refused to respond.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: My experience is based on the contacts that I had with people who -- both those who responded and those who did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that, at the time, that was a legal obligation of every conscript?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I did not know what legal obligation was at the time; therefore, I cannot provide any positive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that, should one refuse to receive call-up papers, these persons could be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I personally never refused to receive call-up papers; therefore, I was not aware of consequences should one refuse to do so, and I'm not knowledgeable about these processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This attitude of non-Serb population towards the JNA, was that something that made the JNA, at one point in time, a single ethnic army?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What would you put it like?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the Yugoslav People's Army was never mono-ethnic, but that the majority, nevertheless, was by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can agree that the majority part of the population of Yugoslavia were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know, then, that the majority members of the JNA were Serbs? You just said that a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience, because I served in the JNA. I served for 11 months. And over that period, I met many people who were in the JNA, most of them were Serbs, of Serbian religion. When I say "the majority," I'm not saying that I counted them or that I learned some percentages. But the majority of people I met there, and befriended were Serbs, and I didn't mind that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chambers fails to see on many of your questions what the relevance is. And for some other questions, it appears that the witness has no specific knowledge about it, such as the composition of the JNA, for example. So, therefore, would you please move on. Come to questions which are both relevant and where the witness can -- has knowledge to answer your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at paragraph 8 of your statement. In the last sentence of that paragraph of your statement, P434, you say that: "After period of time there was a move towards establishing separate police stations." Can you please explain how these separate police stations were established.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, in Rogatica town and in the general area, a territorial creation was made, which was called Republika Srpska. So as part of that territory, town of Rogatica was integrated into it. This creation was not established through any kind of elections or through opinion polls conducted among the population. It was called the Serbian republic, which means that the majority of non-Serb population started feeling as second-rate citizens. Following the establishment of that territorial unit, was establishment of institutions, and one of those institutions was the police of Republika Srpska. So in addition to the existing police force of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the police of Republika Srpska was also created. And immediately after that, the building in which the BH police was headquartered was literally partitioned by a wall, and in one half of that building the police of Republika Srpska was housed and it was made up of former members of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were of the Serbian ethnicity. So in the very small territory of the Rogatica town there were two police forces. One of them was the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the other was the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we please look at document D176.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whilst we're waiting for this document to appear, can you remember until which --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. We don't have document D176.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D176. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look now at -- but before that, I began my question by saying until what time you remained part of the professional force of the police?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I remained until the end of March or early April. I cannot remember exactly, but I think that was the time when I left the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 4 of this document. It is a document issued by the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Delimustafic, and in this document he is addressing all public security stations and all security services centre and the SUP of Sarajevo and is conveying an order by the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he says as follows: "Swiftly plan and launch combat operations throughout the territory of the Republic of BH and co-ordinate them with the Territorial Defence staff of the region, district, and Republic of BH, planning combat operations, provide for extensive measures of protection of the people and property of citizens of the Republic of BH." Now my question is the following: At any point after this date, did you see anything of these activities as described or as requested by the minister of the interior and the TO staff in this order?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: If I look at the date of this document, it's 29th of April, 1992. As I said in my previous response I said that I left the police duty in early April. Therefore, I'm not able to give you an answer to this question because, quite simply, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that you were in Rogatica until the 7th of June, when you were practically taken into custody or arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, from April until the 7th of June, did you have an opportunity to hear or see any of the activities mentioned in this order and requested to be implemented by the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I'm going to ask you whether the name of Ramiz Alajbegovic rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of duties he carried out in that period, April, May, June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: In that particular period of time, I could not say what his duties were. The only thing I can say to you is that as far as I know, Ramiz Alajbegovic was deputy commander of the police forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time did you hear that already in June 1992 he had established a unit that held part of the territory of the municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at document P434 again; paragraph 15 more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you say there. Paragraph 15, please. This is what you say there: "About 20 days before the attack on Rogatica," if I understand things correctly, this was on the 25th of May, "two separate Crisis Staffs were established, one was predominantly Muslim, the other predominantly Serb. Each one of them had three to four members respectively." How come you know about the existence of these Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: As for the existence of Crisis Staffs, I found out about that as I talked to my friends in town. Basically it was a small town, a very small town. And this was the ruling principle. If anything happened to anyone, people would hear about it. Since that was a topical things at the time, that these Crisis Staffs were being organised, I heard from some people that were Crisis Staffs were organised on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say on both sides, on these two sides, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Republika Srpska and the Crisis Staff for the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your answer, when you said that it was a small town and that the principle on which things functioned was, I have heard, et cetera, did you, at any point in time while you were in Rogatica, have information to the effect that through the chief of the public security station, Ismet Osmanovic, activities were taken to organise the Muslims in a military way to obtain and bring in weapons and distribute these weapons in Rogatica basically through ethnic Muslims. Have you heard of this information?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to ask you the following: Is it correct that Ismet Osmanovic at the time was the chief of the public security station in Rogatica where you worked?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I'm asking you is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pause between question and answer, and between answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to hear or find out in a way which you describe here that members of the police station or, rather, of the public security station in Rogatica, Ragib Hodzic [phoen] and Mujo Satrovic [phoen], if I'm reading this correctly, and Mrdjan Gakovic [phoen] were person who were actively involved in the Crisis Staff of the SDA, in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. I did not hear that. As I've already said, I left the police force of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Rogatica for a single reason: Not to be drawn into any kind of conflict, political conflict, armed conflict, or any kind of debate within Rogatica. In that way, I basically separated myself from all the developments that took place after I left. I can only confirm what happened to me personally and what I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is my understanding of the situation, too, but you said this, and that is why I wanted to ask you this question: Whether the principle upon which you functioned in Rogatica was I have heard such and such a thing because it was a small town. If this is your answer, then I'm not going to put any other questions to you in this regard because I know that it would amount to hearsay. Now let us look at paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, for your information, the Chamber has decided that we'll not take another break, and that we will continue and stop at 2.15 sharp to the extent that it would be possible to conclude cross-examination by then, you're invited to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at paragraph 17. You say, inter alia, that on the 25th of May, 1992, when the conflict broke out in Rogatica, there may have been 50 to 70 armed Muslims in Rogatica and that part of these weapons were obtained through private channels. Do you know this? Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: When I say "through private channels," I mean that the weapons that people had were basically hunting guns that were used for sports, for hunting, or there were individual pistols that a minority had from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what my question was. Please take a look at this. Fifty to 70 armed persons; you say that. Is that based on your personal knowledge? Did you see that yourself? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you say that kind of thing to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I knew the people had weapons, but I did not see 50 or 70 persons in a single spot; 50 or 70 persons who were armed, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, "through private channels," is that still in paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I have a problem with the translation. In B/C/S, it says: "Part of the weapons were obtained through private channels."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that not the redacted part of paragraph 17, which is replaced by Adjudicated Fact 1128?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But since I thought that this is something that this Defence would challenge I wanted to put this question: How come the witness had this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the knowledge of the witness of adjudicated fact seems not to be relevant anymore, just the adjudicated fact itself. And if you refer to any portion of paragraph 17 which is meanwhile redacted, then at least you were expected to indicate that clearly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But this is what I'm going to ask you now: Did you then have an opportunity to see these armed men in -- at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity of seeing some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you say that I'm right if I put it to you that, then, just before the 25th of May, 1992, the Serb population from Rogatica had fled Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of the Serb population of Rogatica had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I'm going to ask you whether you know the reason why the Serb population left Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at P166. While we're waiting for this document, Your Honours, I would just like to say that this is a document that bears the date of the 23rd of May, 1992, and it was signed by Rajko Kusic, who has been mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, I would like to ask you that we take a look at this document together. So this is the 23rd of May, 1992. And it says that the commander of the battalion of the SO Rogatica. Can this abbreviation assist you in any way? Can you tell us what this stands for, SO?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that on the 22nd of May, there was firing against enemy strongholds. In Dub Pokrivenik enemy strongholds of Dub Pokrivenik, Kopljevici, Kozici, and Cadovi and also against Pasica Kula, Rajs Laze and the Rudo 2 settlement. And then it says as for the parts of town of Rajs Laze and Rudo 2, an infantry attack was launched against these areas. Please tell us, these names, Rajs Laze, Rudo 2, do they say anything to you? Are these neighbourhoods in Rogatica? Are these parts of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Rudo 2 and Laze were neighbourhoods outside the town of Rogatica, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say or, rather, would you please tell the Court what the population was there in those areas in these neighbourhoods on the outskirts of town?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I cannot really say. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to conclude by putting the following question: An infantry attack was launched here - that's what it says - did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to deal with this document any longer then. It was my understanding that it was on the 7th of June, 1992, that you were brought into custody; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I was arrested. I was taken prisoner in the beginning of June. I can no longer remember the exact date. I believe it was the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were arrested by policemen and amongst them you recognised two of them, Slavisa Vukojcic and Milisav Ivanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before this happened, as you describe things here, you returned the weapons that you had received as a policeman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But part of these service weapons or, rather, the pistol that you had had issued to you, did you return that as well?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: A pistol is not a service weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you had a pistol of your own, privately owned?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I inherited a pistol from my father upon his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This pistol was seized from you in the presence of your colleague, an employee of the police station in Rogatica. His name is Vlado Markovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked with Vlado Markovic, and he is the one who took the pistol away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While that happened, and while you went to your apartment, Vlado Markovic was fair towards you. He treated you in a correct manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the next 20 days, you were in the building of the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is also where the police provided security, the police commanded precisely by Vlado Markovic yet again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself in the building of the school in Rogatica there were quite a few women and children from Rogatica there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber roughly what your estimate may be, how many people were in the school at the time.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: My estimate is approximately 300 men, children, and -- women, children, and elderly men, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the 20 days that you spent there, you were guarded by the police force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: We were guarded by the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that period, you were allowed to go out, to neighbouring houses, to do the shopping, to buy foodstuffs and hygiene items, and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No. Only specific individuals had permit to leave during a specific period of time to go to the neighbouring houses and to try and find if there were any food left in those houses so that they could bring it to the people who were detained at the secondary school. All the shops were closed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to procure a cooker and fuel so that you can cook your meals in the secondary school building?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was only one cooker there and it had been brought from a nearby house. It was being used to prepare food for 300 prisoners who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at paragraph 27; Exhibit P434. It's your statement, Mr. Pasic, which was admitted into evidence in this case, and, there, you say, among other things. We're going to wait for the B/C/S version to appear as well. Somewhere in the middle you say: "Then we were permitted to take three stoves from neighbouring houses. They let us prepare meals in the school building. Women prisoners were allowed to leave the school building to fetch supplies in town." So what is correct? This, what is written in your statement, or your evidence that you gave a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, both. We were allowed to go out and bring in three cookers. However, only one was obtained. As I said, certain individuals, mostly women, were allowed during a certain period of time to go out and try to fetch food in order to prepare meals for the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Money was not confiscated from you, and, therefore, you were able to buy cigarettes on the black market; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't have any money on me, and I didn't buy any cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you saw. Did you have an opportunity seeing other detainees buying various commodities, including cigarettes from street vendors?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. On a couple of occasions I saw people buying cigarettes from the soldiers who were guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point while the shelling was in progress, the guards let you leave the school building in order to visit your girlfriend in town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: During a break in the shelling, I was told that I should go to town and to ask a number of people to come and join us at the secondary school building, including my girlfriend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were at Veljko Vlahovic school, you personally were not physically abused or maltreated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify a dilemma that I have and that stems from paragraphs 29 and 30 of your statement. To the best of your knowledge, how long you stayed at the secondary school building, Veljko Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I spent 20-odd days at the secondary school, Veljko Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you about this is that in that context we should look at paragraph 30 of your statement, P434, where you say exactly as you said today as well, and I quote: "On the 27th of June, we were all picked up and the transfer began." And then in paragraph 29 you say that you were detained on the school premises from June 7 to June 27 of 1992. Can you see that? Can we then agree that practically, if this date 27th of June is correct, you spent about 20 days there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I stayed there until June 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if -- when you say in paragraph 29 "until the 17th of June" is a mistake; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I believe that's a misprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the original because in English it says 27th. And apparently this is it mistranslated. Because the English seems to be the original. Therefore, Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has carefully monitored your cross-examination until now, Mr. Stojanovic, and the Chamber expects you in view of relevance and issues raised to prioritise the most important matters and to finish by ten minutes past 2.00 so that Mr. Jeremy has another five minutes for re-examination. If you need any time for that, Mr. Jeremy. Would you need any?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Not at this moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment. Then we'll at least establish whether this has changed at ten minutes past 2.00. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were taken from the Veljko Vlahovic school again by members, as you say, special police forces, to a farm where Vlado Markovic's headquarters was also housed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the premises of former agricultural farm at the exit point of Rogatica town. Two or three days later, we were able to conclude that also on the premises were the headquarters of the forces that had captured us and were guarding us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are again talking about the same police forces that you spoke about earlier and who were led by Vlado Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Those were mixed forces. There was police. There was army. And apparently Vlado Markovic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay there, at this farm, you were not physically abused or maltreated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then, on the 15th of July, to the best of your recollection, you were driven towards Vlasenica and Kladanj until the place called Tistje, which is located on the separation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: We were told that we were going to be exchanged and allowed to go to the territory controlled by some other forces; specifically the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. En route, we were stopped at Tistje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why you were not exchanged on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your position? What did you wish at that moment? What were you willing to do at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: You mean when we were at Tistje?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both whilst you were on the farm and when you headed off towards Tistje.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: While we were on the farm, I was under a false impression that I would be allowed to continue living in my native town as a loyal resident. However, that was not something that was going to be permitted for me to do because I was under suspicion. Once we left Rogatica, and once we were told that we would be exchanged, my only aim was to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Practically you spent night in Susica near Vlasenica. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you were sent to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were transferred to the Batkovici camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Stojanovic, you apparently read portions of the statement in the last ten minutes right -- I mean, the witness has testified to that. So, therefore, unless there is any reason why you would expect him to change his mind, there's no need to do that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at paragraph 41 of your statement; Exhibit P434. Mr. Pasic, I'm going to put a few questions to you about Batkovic, but before that, I would like just to present the Defence case to you. You cannot recall all the details relating to Batkovic. You can only assume who performed which duties. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with what you said. I'm talking about what I saw and what I know. I'm making no assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 41 where you say that when you arrived, the chief of the camp was a man by the name of Veljo. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, can you tell us how long did he perform this duty of camp warden until he was replaced by a person called Drago?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: A few weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What you say in paragraph 41, that the camp warden had the rank of a sergeant and that was the most senior non-commissioned officer rank in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my conclusion, based on the insignia that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And he performed the duties of the camp warden with that specific rank?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then, in paragraph 42, you say, among other things: "One night, approximately in mid-August 1992, a man from Bijeljina, about 35 years of age, known to us as Professor, was taken from the hangar building to the open compound area." And then you go on to describe his death. This date, or this period, mid-August, is this something that you are sure about, or is it your -- is this your assumption?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I wasn't assuming anything. I said this to the best of my recollection. And that's exactly why I said mid-August, because I cannot say for sure whether it was the 5th or the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But that was not in July?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at Exhibit D47.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- I apologise. D267. 1D267. Whilst we are waiting, let me tell you, Your Honours, that this is a -- the indictment that we had an occasion to see earlier in courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... D267. Yes, it's MFI'd as D47.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are still waiting for the translation. That's why it was only MFI'd. And, with your leave, I would use the interpreters in the booth, in order to go through these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to a limited extent, with the indulgence of the interpreters, we may go on that path, although it's not common. But could you then please come to your point as quickly as possible. If it is about the date, then let's deal with the date immediately. To the extent you could not agree with the Prosecution on dates mentioned in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to take a look at page 3 of this document. You saw the first page, and you saw that four persons were indicted and their names were mentioned on page 1. The warden, the deputy warden of the camp in Batkovic. And it says that they were also responsible for the following: "Due to the beatings administered, the following persons were killed: Zecevic Ferid, nicknamed Professor, passed away on 28 July 1992." Do you see that? Do you see that, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This date, in connection with which four persons were indicted, would that be the exact date of the Professor's death, or is what you are telling us correct; namely, mid-August?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I had been in captivity for quite a long time before this happened. I had seen terrible things happen. If I misstated the date, I think that it was possible that I made a mistake in terms of a week or two. This was the end of July, and I said that it was August. So a ten-day difference doesn't make this less correct. To the best of my recollection, it happened in the beginning of August, or in mid-August ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The point is -- the point --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point seems to be clear is that there's a different date here than in the indictment. Please move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 45 -- actually, Your Honours, to be as practical as possible, I will try to fit into the time allocated to us. While we're still on this page, let us take a look at this indictment. And does it not say here that in the period that is mentioned in the indictment, the period during which you were in Batkovici, six persons, six prisoners succumbed to the beatings administered to them. And then their names are listed. You can see that, can you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could we first ask: Have you ever seen this indictment before, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the indictment says, Mr. Stojanovic, I take it, certainly after it has been translated, you could agree on that, I take it, with the Prosecution -- well, as long as it comes to Professor and the 28th of July, it is not that difficult to find it, and even for us to read it on page 2. But let's not go through a document -- unless you have any specific question to this witness about something which is described here, point at that portion, ask the question, and then move on. But we shouldn't go with this witness through an indictment. That is not assisting the Chamber. Certainly if he has not seen that indictment ever before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. And I shall be done with this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw the names: Sutic, Husein; Zecevic, Ferid; Okanovic, Iljaz; Hadziomerevic, Zulfo; Topcic, Idriz; and Habibovic, Sead. Now I would like to ask that we look at paragraph 45 of your statement, which is P434. This is what you say there: "During the first two months of my detention at Batkovic ..." You say that you had the occasion to know that Mehmed Hodzic and Hamdo, whose last name you don't know, were beaten very badly and that they died as a result of the injuries sustained during the beatings. Do you stand by this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to ask you this: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber where you were and where you watched this from.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: While I was in camp Batkovic, during the first two months before we were registered by the Red Cross, it would often happen that soldiers would come from the front line, enter the camp, and do whatever they wanted. For the most part, they came to take things out on prisoners. Actually, express their rage in that way against the prisoners. At first, we were in a big military tent within the camp compound, and, on one day, among other things, these soldiers came, and they beat and mistreat all the prisoners who were in that tent. The prisoners were mistreated in a variety of ways. The prisoners included these two elderly men whom I knew from Rogatica. On that same day, later on, both of these men died. They were taken out. They were carried out of the camp compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you saw this and where you were when you saw this, in which facility?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: I was in this tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this personally?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
